title: 08 — System Design (HLD)
html:
08 — System Design (HLD)

What HLD actually is: deciding the components, their responsibilities, how they communicate, where state lives, and how the whole thing behaves when parts fail — with numbers, not adjectives.

1. The interview framework (also the real-work framework)

45 minutes, roughly:

flowchart TD
    A["1. Requirements — 5 min<br/>functional + non-functional + out of scope"] --> B["2. Estimation — 5 min<br/>QPS, storage, bandwidth"]
    B --> C["3. API contract — 3 min<br/>the 3-5 operations that matter"]
    C --> D["4. Data model — 5 min<br/>entities, access patterns, store choice"]
    D --> E["5. High-level diagram — 10 min<br/>components and dataflow"]
    E --> F["6. Deep dive — 12 min<br/>the 2 hardest parts"]
    F --> G["7. Bottlenecks, failure modes,<br/>trade-offs — 5 min"]

Step 1 — the questions to ask, every time:

Category Questions
Scope Which features are in scope? What can I explicitly ignore? Who are the users?
Scale DAU/MAU? Reads vs writes ratio? Peak vs average? Growth over 2 years?
Data How much per item? Retention? Is old data cold? PII/regulated?
Consistency Can a user see stale data? For how long? Is it OK to lose the last second of writes?
Latency p50/p99 target for each operation?
Availability SLO? What's the cost of an hour of downtime?
Geography Single region or global? Data residency constraints?

⚠️ The #1 interview failure is jumping to boxes before establishing scale. A design for 1,000 users and one for 100M users are different designs, and picking the second for the first problem is also a wrong answer.

Step 7 — always end with: "Here's what breaks first as we grow, here's what I'd monitor, and here's the trade-off I chose and what I'd change if requirement X were different."

2. Estimation — the numbers and the arithmetic

2.1 Constants worth memorising

Seconds per day        ≈ 86,400  ≈ 10^5
1 million/day          ≈ 12 QPS
1 billion/day          ≈ 12,000 QPS
Peak                   ≈ 2–3× average (spikier for consumer apps: 5–10×)
1 char (ASCII)         = 1 byte;  UTF-8 typical text ≈ 1–2 B/char
UUID                   = 16 B binary, 36 B as string
Timestamp (long)       = 8 B
A "row" of metadata    ≈ 100–1000 B
1 KB × 1M              = 1 GB;   1 KB × 1B = 1 TB
1 MB × 1M              = 1 TB;   1 MB × 1B = 1 PB
Commodity server       ≈ 64–256 GB RAM, 8–64 cores, 1–10 Gbps NIC
One SQL box realistic  ≈ 5–10k simple QPS, ~1–5 TB comfortably
Redis single node      ≈ 100k+ ops/s
Kafka broker           ≈ 100s of MB/s

2.2 Worked example — a Twitter-scale feed

300M MAU, 50% daily active           → 150M DAU
Each posts 0.5 tweets/day            → 75M tweets/day  ≈ 900 writes/s (peak ~2700/s)
Each reads feed 10×/day              → 1.5B reads/day  ≈ 17k reads/s (peak ~50k/s)
Read:write ratio                     ≈ 20:1  → READ-HEAVY: cache + fan-out on write

Storage:
  tweet = 280 chars (~560 B UTF-8) + metadata 200 B ≈ 800 B → round to 1 KB
  75M × 1 KB = 75 GB/day → 27 TB/year → 5 years = 135 TB (before replication)
  With media: 10% have a 200 KB image → 7.5M × 200 KB = 1.5 TB/day → object storage, not the DB

Bandwidth:
  Write: 900/s × 1 KB       = ~1 MB/s          (trivial)
  Read:  17k/s × 20 tweets × 1 KB = 340 MB/s   (this is the real cost → CDN + cache)

Cache sizing (80/20 rule): 20% of tweets serve 80% of reads
  daily hot set ≈ 75M × 20% × 1 KB = 15 GB → fits in a small Redis cluster easily

The point of estimation is not precision. It's to discover which dimension is the problem. Here: reads, and specifically read bandwidth — which immediately tells you the architecture (aggressive caching, fan-out on write, CDN for media).

3. The building blocks

flowchart TB
    C["Clients<br/>web · mobile · API"] --> DNS[DNS / GSLB]
    DNS --> CDN[CDN — static + media]
    DNS --> LB[Load balancer]
    LB --> GW[API gateway<br/>authN · rate limit · routing]
    GW --> S1[Service A<br/>stateless]
    GW --> S2[Service B<br/>stateless]
    S1 --> CA[(Cache — Redis)]
    S1 --> DB[(Primary DB<br/>+ read replicas)]
    S1 --> Q[[Message queue]]
    Q --> W[Workers]
    W --> DB
    W --> OS[(Object storage)]
    S2 --> SE[(Search index)]
    DB -.CDC.-> DW[(Analytics / warehouse)]
    ALL[All components] -.-> OBS[Metrics · Logs · Traces]

Responsibility of each, in one line:

Component Job Failure behaviour to design
CDN Serve bytes near the user Origin shield; stale-while-revalidate on origin failure
Load balancer Distribute + health-check Removes unhealthy instances; needs ≥2 AZs itself
API gateway Auth, rate limit, route, aggregate Fail closed on auth, fail open on optional enrichment
Stateless service Business logic Any instance can die; horizontal scale
Cache Absorb read load Must survive a cold cache — see §5.4
Primary DB System of record Failover to replica; RPO/RTO defined
Queue Decouple, level load, retry DLQ, idempotent consumers
Object storage Large blobs 11-nines durability; serve via signed URLs, never proxy through the API
Search index Text/faceted queries Rebuildable from source of truth

4. Scaling: the levers in order of preference

flowchart LR
    A[Too slow / too much load] --> B[1. Measure — find the actual bottleneck]
    B --> C[2. Optimise: indexes, query plans,<br/>N+1, payload size, algorithms]
    C --> D[3. Cache: CDN → app → query → object]
    D --> E[4. Scale vertically — biggest box]
    E --> F[5. Scale horizontally — stateless + LB]
    F --> G[6. Read replicas]
    G --> H[7. Async: queue the non-critical work]
    H --> I[8. Partition/shard the data]
    I --> J[9. Denormalise / separate read models]
    J --> K[10. Multi-region]

Do them in order. Each step down costs more complexity than the one above. Most systems that "need sharding" actually need an index.

4.1 Vertical vs horizontal

Vertical Horizontal
How Bigger machine More machines
Limit Hardware ceiling, cost curve is superlinear ~unlimited
Complexity None State, consistency, coordination, deployment
Availability SPOF Redundant by construction
Use Databases first (a 96-core box is astonishingly capable), simplicity Stateless tiers always

Underrated advice: vertical scaling the database and horizontal scaling everything else takes you much further than most people assume. Stack Overflow famously ran on a handful of servers.

4.2 Statelessness — the enabling property

For a service to scale horizontally, no request may depend on which instance handles it. Move state out:

State Where it goes
Session Redis / signed cookie / JWT
Uploaded files Object storage
In-memory cache Distributed cache (or accept per-instance cache with short TTL)
Scheduled jobs A distributed scheduler with leader election, or a queue
WebSocket connections Sticky + backplane (Redis / Azure SignalR)
Locks / counters Redis / database

4.3 Database replication

flowchart LR
    W[Writes] --> P[(Primary)]
    P -->|async replication| R1[(Replica 1)]
    P -->|async replication| R2[(Replica 2)]
    RD[Reads] --> R1
    RD --> R2
Mode Guarantee Cost
Async Primary commits immediately Replica lag → stale reads; data loss window on failover
Semi-sync ≥1 replica acknowledged Higher write latency, bounded loss
Sync All replicas acknowledged Highest latency, no loss, availability drops (any replica down blocks writes)

⚠️ Read-your-own-writes: a user posts a comment, is redirected, reads from a lagging replica, and their comment is missing. Fixes: route a user's reads to the primary for N seconds after a write; sticky routing by session; or return the written entity from the write endpoint and render it optimistically.

4.4 Sharding (horizontal partitioning)

Strategy Key Pros Cons
Range A–M, N–Z, or by date Range scans efficient Hotspots — today's date shard takes all writes
Hash hash(key) % N Even distribution Range queries hit all shards; resharding moves everything
Consistent hash Hash ring + vnodes Adding a node moves only ~1/N Slightly more complex
Directory/lookup A mapping service Flexible, easy rebalancing The lookup service is a SPOF and an extra hop
Geographic By region Latency + data residency Cross-region queries expensive

Choosing a shard key — the most consequential decision:

  1. High cardinality (many distinct values).
  2. Even distribution (no celebrity/whale skew).
  3. Matches the dominant query — if you shard orders by OrderId but always query by CustomerId, every query is a scatter-gather across all shards.
  4. Stable — a value that never changes (moving a row between shards is painful).

⚠️ What sharding costs you: cross-shard joins (do them in the app or denormalise), cross-shard transactions (2PC is slow and fragile — use sagas), global uniqueness (use Snowflake IDs or per-shard ranges, not auto-increment), rebalancing, and much harder operations. Shard last.

Snowflake ID — the standard distributed ID:

 64 bits:  [1 unused][41 bits timestamp ms][10 bits machine id][12 bits sequence]
 → time-sortable, no coordination, 4096 IDs/ms/machine, ~69 years of range

Alternatives: UUIDv7 (time-ordered UUID, index-friendly, no coordination), ULID, or a DB ticket server (simple, a SPOF).

5. Caching — the highest-leverage technique

5.1 Where caches live

Browser cache → CDN → API gateway cache → Application in-memory → Distributed (Redis) → DB buffer pool → OS page cache
   fastest, least fresh  ──────────────────────────────────────────────▶  slowest, most fresh

5.2 Patterns

Pattern Flow Use Watch out
Cache-aside (lazy) App checks cache → miss → read DB → populate Default. Simple, resilient to cache loss First request always slow; stale on external writes
Read-through Cache library loads on miss Cleaner app code Needs a cache that supports it
Write-through Write cache + DB synchronously Cache always fresh Slower writes; caches data that may never be read
Write-behind Write cache, flush to DB async Fast writes, absorbs bursts Data loss if the cache dies; complexity
Refresh-ahead Proactively refresh before expiry Hot keys never miss Wasted work on cold keys 
// Cache-aside with stampede protection and jittered TTL — the production shape
public async Task<Quote> GetQuoteAsync(string symbol, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var key = $"quote:v1:{symbol}";
    if (_cache.TryGetValue(key, out Quote? cached) && cached is not null)
        return cached;

    // One loader per key: prevents N concurrent misses hammering the DB (stampede)
    var gate = _locks.GetOrAdd(key, _ => new SemaphoreSlim(1, 1));
    await gate.WaitAsync(ct);
    try
    {
        if (_cache.TryGetValue(key, out cached) && cached is not null) return cached;  // double-check

        var quote = await _repository.GetQuoteAsync(symbol, ct);
        // Jitter prevents thousands of keys expiring in the same second
        var ttl = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(60 + Random.Shared.Next(0, 15));
        _cache.Set(key, quote, ttl);
        return quote;
    }
    finally { gate.Release(); }
}

5.3 Invalidation

"There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things." — Phil Karlton

Strategy How Trade-off
TTL Expire after N seconds Simple, bounded staleness. Start here
Explicit delete on write Writer removes the key Fresh, but easy to miss a write path; race conditions
Write-through Update the cache on write Fresh; only works if you own all writers
Versioned keys quote:v2:{sym}; bump the version to invalidate everything Atomic mass invalidation, no delete storm
Event-driven Subscribe to CDC/domain events, invalidate Works across services; adds a dependency

Recommendation: TTL + explicit invalidation on the write paths you own + a version prefix for schema changes. And always state the acceptable staleness window — it's a product decision, not a technical one.

5.4 Cache failure modes (know these by name)

Failure Cause Mitigation
Stampede / dogpile Hot key expires; 10k requests miss simultaneously Per-key lock (above), stale-while-revalidate, probabilistic early expiry
Avalanche Many keys expire at once (e.g. all set at deploy time) Jitter the TTLs
Penetration Requests for keys that don't exist bypass the cache to the DB every time (often an attack) Cache the negative result briefly; Bloom filter of known keys
Hot key One key gets 50% of traffic (celebrity problem) Local L1 cache in front of Redis; key replication (key:1..N)
Big key A 50 MB value blocks Redis (single-threaded) Split it; never store huge blobs in Redis
Cold start Cache cluster restarts; the DB gets 100% of traffic and dies Capacity-plan the DB for a cold cache, or warm it before taking traffic. This has caused major outages
Inconsistency Cache updated, DB write rolled back Invalidate after commit, never before; or use the outbox

6. Consistency, CAP, and what to actually say

6.1 CAP, stated correctly

During a network partition you must choose Consistency (reject requests that can't be made consistent) or Availability (answer, possibly with stale data). When there's no partition, you get both. CAP is about the partition case only.

PACELC is the more useful formulation:

if Partition → choose Availability or Consistency; Else (normal operation) → choose Latency or Consistency.

Most real systems are PA/EL (Cassandra, DynamoDB default, Cosmos default) or PC/EC (traditional RDBMS, Spanner).

6.2 Consistency models

Model Guarantee Example
Linearizable / strong Every read sees the latest committed write, globally etcd, Spanner, a single RDBMS
Sequential All nodes see operations in the same order —
Causal Causally related operations are seen in order Collaborative editing
Read-your-writes You always see your own writes Session stickiness
Monotonic reads You never see time go backwards Sticky replica routing
Eventual Given no new writes, replicas converge... eventually DNS, S3 (historically), Cassandra

How to answer "which consistency do you need?" in a design: per operation, not per system. "Payment authorisation: strong. Feed ranking: eventual with a 5-second window. Profile updates: read-your-writes for the author, eventual for everyone else." That level of specificity is a senior signal.

6.3 Distributed transactions

Approach Guarantee Cost Use
Local transaction ACID None Single DB — always prefer
2PC / XA Atomic across resources Blocking on coordinator failure, slow, poor availability Legacy enterprise; avoid in new designs
Saga Eventual atomicity via compensation No isolation; visible intermediate states The standard microservices answer
Outbox + idempotent consumer At-least-once delivery, exactly-once effect Extra table + relay Use this for reliable event publishing, always

6.4 Consensus (know the shape, not the proof)

Raft — a leader is elected; all writes go to the leader; the leader replicates to followers; an entry commits when a majority (quorum) acknowledges. Tolerates ⌊(N−1)/2⌋ failures → use odd node counts (3 tolerates 1, 5 tolerates 2).

Quorum arithmetic: with N replicas, write quorum W and read quorum R, W + R > N guarantees a read sees the latest write. Common: N=3, W=2, R=2. Tune for read-heavy (W=3, R=1) or write-heavy (W=1, R=3).

Where consensus shows up: leader election, distributed locks, cluster membership, configuration (etcd/ZooKeeper/Consul), and the internals of Kafka controllers, Kubernetes, CockroachDB, Spanner. ⚠️ Don't implement it. Use a system that already has it.

7. Rate limiting

Algorithm Behaviour Memory Notes
Fixed window Count per calendar window O(1) ⚠️ Allows a 2× burst at the boundary
Sliding window log Timestamps of every request O(requests) Exact, expensive
Sliding window counter Weighted blend of current + previous window O(1) Good approximation. Common default
Token bucket Tokens refill at rate R, capacity B O(1) Allows controlled bursts — usually what you want
Leaky bucket Requests drain at a constant rate O(1) Smooths output; queues rather than rejects 
// Distributed token bucket in Redis — atomic via Lua, no race between check and decrement
private const string TokenBucketScript = """
    local key      = KEYS[1]
    local rate     = tonumber(ARGV[1])   -- tokens per second
    local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[2])
    local now      = tonumber(ARGV[3])   -- caller-supplied clock (ms)
    local cost     = tonumber(ARGV[4])

    local bucket = redis.call('HMGET', key, 'tokens', 'ts')
    local tokens = tonumber(bucket[1]) or capacity
    local ts     = tonumber(bucket[2]) or now

    tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + (now - ts) / 1000 * rate)
    local allowed = tokens >= cost
    if allowed then tokens = tokens - cost end

    redis.call('HMSET', key, 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
    redis.call('PEXPIRE', key, math.ceil(capacity / rate * 1000) * 2)
    return { allowed and 1 or 0, tostring(tokens) }
    """;

Design points: limit per identity (API key/user/tenant), not per IP alone (NAT shares IPs). Always return 429 with Retry-After, X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset. Apply at the gateway for coarse protection and in-service for per-tenant fairness. .NET 7+ has built-in AddRateLimiter with all four algorithms.

8. Case studies

8.1 URL shortener (the canonical warm-up)

Requirements: shorten a URL, redirect, ~100M new URLs/day, 10:1 read:write, 5-year retention, custom aliases optional, analytics optional.

Estimation: 100M/day ≈ 1,200 writes/s, 12,000 reads/s (peak ~35k/s). 5 years × 365 × 100M = 182B URLs → need ≥ 62^7 (62⁷ = 3.5T, 7 chars is enough; 62⁶ = 56B is not). Storage: 182B × 500 B ≈ 91 TB.

Key design decision — how to generate the short code: | Option | Pros | Cons | |---|---|---| | Hash(URL) + take 7 chars | Deduplicates identical URLs | Collisions must be detected and resolved | | Random 7 chars | Simple, unguessable | Collision check needed; retry loop | | Counter → base62 | No collisions, shortest codes | Sequential = enumerable (privacy leak); needs a distributed counter | | Pre-generated key pool | O(1) issue, no collisions, unguessable if shuffled | A key-generation service to operate | Choice: counter-based with a per-node range allocation (each node grabs 10,000 IDs at a time from a central allocator) then base62-encode with a bijective scramble to avoid enumeration. States the trade-off: unguessability vs simplicity.

POST /api/urls  {"url":"https://...", "alias":"optional", "expiresAt":"..."}  → 201 {shortUrl}
GET  /{code}    → 301/302 to the long URL

⚠️ 301 vs 302: 301 (permanent) is cached by browsers → fast, but you lose all click analytics and can't change the target. Use 302 if analytics matter. This is the classic "did you think about it" question.

flowchart LR
    U[User] --> CDN[CDN/edge]
    CDN --> LB --> API[Redirect service<br/>stateless]
    API --> C[(Redis: code → URL<br/>hot set, LRU)]
    C -.miss.-> DB[(Key-value store<br/>sharded by code hash)]
    W[Write service] --> IDGEN[ID range allocator]
    W --> DB
    API -->|async| Q[[Click events queue]] --> AN[(Analytics store)]

Why a KV store: the only access pattern is point lookup by code. Cassandra/DynamoDB shards trivially by the code. No joins, no transactions. Cache hit rate: Zipf distribution — a small hot set serves most traffic; 20 GB of Redis probably serves >90%. Failure modes: cache cold start (capacity-plan the KV store for it); the ID allocator is a SPOF (make it a replicated service, and nodes hold a local range so a brief outage is invisible).

8.2 Rate limiter as a service

Covered in §7. Design points for the service version: a Redis cluster sharded by the limit key; the gateway calls it in-line (needs sub-ms p99 → colocate) or applies a local token bucket synced periodically (approximate but never adds latency). State the trade-off: exactness vs latency vs blast radius.

8.3 News feed (fan-out)

The core decision:

Fan-out on write (push) Fan-out on read (pull)
On post Write to every follower's feed list Just store the post
On read Read one precomputed list — fast Query all followees and merge — slow
Cost Expensive for users with 50M followers Expensive on every read
Freshness Slight delay for the tail of the fan-out Always current
Best for Most users (few thousand followers) Celebrities

Answer: hybrid. Fan-out on write for normal users; for celebrities (> ~10k followers), don't fan out — merge their posts in at read time. This is what Twitter/Instagram actually do, and saying "hybrid, with a follower-count threshold" is the expected senior answer.

flowchart TB
    P[Post service] --> DB[(Posts DB)]
    P --> Q[[Fan-out queue]]
    Q --> FO[Fan-out workers]
    FO -->|"if followers < 10k"| FEED[(Feed cache per user<br/>Redis list of post IDs, capped at 800)]
    FO -->|"if celebrity: skip"| X[ ]
    R[Feed read service] --> FEED
    R -->|"merge celebrity posts<br/>at read time"| DB
    R --> RANK[Ranking service<br/>ML scoring]

Details that matter: cap the stored feed (~800 IDs — nobody scrolls further); store IDs, hydrate content from a cache; rank asynchronously; handle unfollow/delete by filtering at read (cheaper than rewriting millions of lists).

8.4 Chat / messaging system

Requirements: 1:1 and group chat, delivery + read receipts, online presence, message history, push when offline, 50M DAU.

flowchart TB
    C1[Client A] <-->|WebSocket| GW1[Chat gateway 1<br/>holds connections]
    C2[Client B] <-->|WebSocket| GW2[Chat gateway 2]
    GW1 --> SD[(Session registry<br/>userId → gatewayId, Redis)]
    GW2 --> SD
    GW1 --> MS[Message service]
    MS --> MDB[(Message store<br/>Cassandra, partition by conversationId,<br/>clustered by timestamp DESC)]
    MS --> BUS[[Pub/sub — route to the right gateway]]
    BUS --> GW2
    MS -->|offline| PUSH[Push notification service]
    PR[Presence service] --> SD

Key decisions:

  • WebSocket for bidirectional low latency; fall back to long polling. Gateways are stateful (they hold connections) → the session registry maps user → gateway so any service can route to them.
  • Cassandra/DynamoDB for messages: massive write volume, partition by conversationId, cluster by timestamp DESC so "last 50 messages" is a single sequential read. No joins needed.
  • Ordering: per conversation, assign a monotonic sequence number server-side (client timestamps are unreliable). Clients sort by sequence, not by clock.
  • Delivery guarantees: client sends with a client-generated message ID → server dedupes → at-least-once delivery with idempotency = exactly-once effect. Unacked messages are retried on reconnect.
  • Presence: heartbeat every 30 s, TTL key in Redis; ⚠️ presence fan-out is surprisingly expensive (N² for large groups) — batch it and only push to users currently viewing.
  • Group chat: for small groups, fan out to each member's device. For huge groups/channels, treat it like a feed (pull).

8.5 Distributed job scheduler

Requirements: schedule one-off and recurring jobs, at-least-once execution, retries with backoff, no duplicate execution, visibility.

Design: a jobs table (or a time-partitioned store) with next_run_at; N workers poll with SELECT ... WHERE next_run_at <= now() ORDER BY next_run_at LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED (Postgres) or a leased-message queue. SKIP LOCKED is the key trick — it gives you competing consumers without a distributed lock.

  • Exactly-once is impossible; make jobs idempotent and use at-least-once.
  • Leases, not locks: a worker claims a job with a lease expiry; if it dies, the lease expires and another worker picks it up. Heartbeat to extend for long jobs.
  • Scale to millions of timers: a hierarchical timing wheel rather than a sorted set scan.
  • Recurring jobs: compute the next run on completion, not on schedule creation (prevents drift and pile-up).
  • Poison jobs: max attempts → DLQ + alert.

8.6 Search / autocomplete

  • Inverted index: term → posting list of document IDs (+ positions, frequencies). This is what Elasticsearch/Lucene is.
  • Ranking: BM25 baseline; then learning-to-rank; then personalisation.
  • Autocomplete: trie with top-K completions cached at each node; updated from a query-frequency log (batch, hourly). Serve from memory; typical p99 target < 50 ms.
  • Freshness vs cost: near-real-time indexing (Elasticsearch refresh interval ~1 s) vs batch. State which you need.
  • ⚠️ The search index is not the source of truth — it must be rebuildable from the primary store, and that rebuild must be tested.

8.7 Payment / order processing (correctness over throughput)

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant A as Order API
    participant D as DB
    participant O as Outbox relay
    participant P as Payment provider
    C->>A: POST /orders (Idempotency-Key: abc123)
    A->>D: BEGIN; insert order (unique on idempotency key);<br/>insert outbox row; COMMIT
    A-->>C: 202 Accepted + order id
    O->>D: poll outbox
    O->>P: authorise payment (idempotency key = order id)
    P-->>O: authorised / declined
    O->>D: update order state; insert next outbox event

Non-negotiables: idempotency keys on every mutating endpoint; the transactional outbox so the DB write and the event publish can't diverge; state machine for order status with only legal transitions; never store money in float (use decimal/minor units as integers); full audit log; reconciliation job against the provider's ledger (assume you will diverge and detect it).

8.8 Analytics / metrics pipeline

Producers → Kafka (partitioned by entity) → Stream processor (Flink/Spark/ksqlDB)
    ├→ Real-time aggregates → Redis/Druid → dashboards
    └→ Raw events → object storage (Parquet, partitioned by date) → warehouse
  • Lambda architecture (batch + speed layer) vs Kappa (stream only, replay from the log). Kappa is simpler when your log retention allows replay — prefer it.
  • Late-arriving data: event time vs processing time; watermarks; allowed lateness.
  • Approximate is fine for most dashboards → HyperLogLog for uniques, t-digest for percentiles (file 03 §9).
  • Cardinality is the killer in metrics systems: a label with user IDs in it will destroy Prometheus. Keep label cardinality bounded.

9. Failure modes you must mention unprompted

Failure Design response
A single instance dies Stateless + N≥2 + health checks + auto-restart
An AZ dies Multi-AZ, quorum-aware datastores, no cross-AZ single points
The database is slow Timeouts, connection pool limits, circuit breaker, read replicas, shed load
The cache is empty DB must survive 100% traffic, or warm before serving
A downstream is down Circuit breaker + fallback + queue for later
Traffic spike 10× Autoscaling (with warm-up time!), queue-based load levelling, rate limiting, graceful degradation
A bad deploy Canary + automated rollback on SLO breach + feature flags
Data corruption Backups + PITR + tested restores + immutable audit log
Thundering herd Jitter, backoff, request coalescing, per-key locks
Cascading failure Bulkheads, timeouts shorter than the caller's, load shedding, circuit breakers
Poison message Retry limit → DLQ → alert
Clock skew Never rely on wall clocks for ordering across machines — use logical clocks/sequences

Graceful degradation ladder — decide it in advance, per feature:

Full service → drop personalisation → serve cached/stale → serve static default → read-only mode → maintenance page

10. Answer templates

Trade-off sentence (use it constantly):

"I'd use X because the dominant constraint is Y. That costs us Z, which is acceptable here because reason. If Y changed to Y′, I'd switch to W."

Choosing a datastore, out loud:

"Access pattern is point lookups by key at 50k QPS with no joins → key-value store. If we later need ad-hoc filtering, I'd add a search index fed by CDC rather than change the primary store."

On consistency:

"Writes are strongly consistent within the order aggregate. The read model lags by up to two seconds; the UI shows the user's own change optimistically so they never see their write disappear."

11. Checklist

  • Requirements: functional, non-functional with numbers, explicit out-of-scope
  • Estimation: QPS (avg and peak), storage/year, bandwidth — and the one dimension that dominates
  • API: 3–5 endpoints with real shapes, idempotency where mutating
  • Data model + justified store choice per dataset
  • Diagram: components, protocols, and the direction of data
  • Scaling: which component scales on which signal; the bottleneck order
  • Caching: layer, key, TTL, invalidation, cold-start plan
  • Consistency: stated per operation
  • Failure: per-dependency behaviour, degradation ladder
  • Security: authN/authZ, data classification, tenant isolation
  • Observability: SLIs, key metrics, correlation
  • Cost: rough monthly at target scale
  • Trade-offs: named, with the alternative you rejected and why
